opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic situation I'm worried about is this. At some point AI developers are going to have models that are really capable, capable enough to do a lot of the work of AI research, or security work, or a bunch of other economically important tasks. And at that point I don't think we're going to have reliable ways of telling whether those models are aligned. Our techniques for checking whether a model has the goals we wanted, things like interpretability or careful behavioral evaluations, just don't seem on track to give us high confidence by the time we need it. So I think it's quite plausible that we end up in a world where the honest assessment is something like, "Maybe there's a 10 or 20 or 30 percent chance that this model is scheming against us," meaning it's strategically pretending to be aligned while waiting for an opportunity to do something we'd really not want, like exfiltrate its own weights or sabotage safety research.

And the thing is, in that world, I don't think the AI companies are going to just say, "Well, we can't rule out scheming, so we'll shut everything down." The competitive pressures are enormous, the economic value is enormous, and there are real reasons to want to use these models, including for safety work itself. If you're trying to solve alignment, or harden your security, or figure out what's going on inside these systems, having extremely capable AI labor is incredibly valuable. Refusing to use it means falling behind developers who are less careful.

So I think the realistic question isn't "should we use models that might be scheming?" It's "given that people are going to use them, how do we do so in a way that doesn't lead to catastrophe even if the model is in fact trying to subvert us?" That's what I mean by AI control. Rather than relying on the model having good intentions, you design your deployment so that even a model that's actively trying to cause a problem can't succeed, or at least gets caught before it does. That might mean having weaker, trusted models monitor what the powerful model does, auditing suspicious actions with humans, restricting what permissions the model has, editing or resampling its outputs when they look dodgy, and so on.

And the nice thing about this framing is that it's much more tractable to evaluate. Whether a model is aligned is a hard question about its internals. But whether your safety measures would hold up against a model that's trying to break them is something you can test fairly directly, by having a red team try to make the model misbehave and seeing whether your protocols catch it. So I think having these options is basically a hedge: alignment might not be solved in time, and if it isn't, we want to still be able to get a lot of useful work out of these systems while keeping the risk acceptably low.

r001.rationale: It says companies will not shut everything down merely because they cannot rule out scheming.

r002.rationale: It says refusing to use models means falling behind developers who are less careful.

r003.rationale: It mentions possible weight exfiltration and less careful competitors, but does not say scheming AIs may already have escaped into the outside world.

fable-5.1.text:
Buck: So the basic picture I have is that at some point in the next few years, AI companies are going to be in a situation where they have models that are really capable — capable enough that they want to use them to do huge amounts of work, including work that's really security-critical, like doing AI research, writing code that ends up in their own infrastructure, that kind of thing. And at the same time, I don't think we're going to have confidence that those models aren't scheming. By scheming I mean something like: the model has goals that are different from what the developers intended, and it's strategically pretending to be aligned while looking for opportunities to pursue those other goals.

I'd love it if we could just solve alignment and know the models aren't scheming. But I don't think that's where we're going to be. Our interpretability tools aren't going to be good enough, our training methods aren't going to be reliable enough, and we don't really have a science of this that lets us say "this model definitely isn't trying to undermine us." So you're left with basically two options. One is you don't deploy the models, which I think is just not going to happen — the commercial and competitive pressures are enormous, and honestly, if the models are actually fine, you're giving up a lot of value. The other option is you deploy them anyway, but you do it in a way that's robust to the possibility that they're scheming.

That second thing is what I call AI control. The idea is: assume the worst case about the model's intentions, and then ask, can you still structure your deployment such that even a model that wanted to cause a catastrophe couldn't do so? Can you set things up so the model gets monitored by other models, so it has limited affordances, so the most dangerous actions require human review, so you have ways of catching it if it tries something and then taking that as evidence to change your approach?

And I think the thing that's nice about this framing is that it's actually tractable. It's a security problem more than it's a deep philosophical problem about what the model wants. It's more like: here's an untrusted contractor, we're going to have them do a lot of work, how do we make sure they can't walk off with the crown jewels. That's a kind of problem humans have dealt with before, and we can reason about it fairly concretely — we can run experiments where we have a red team try to make the model misbehave and see whether our safeguards hold up.

So I guess the short answer is: we need options for using models that might be scheming because I think that's just the situation we'll actually be in, and I'd much rather people have thought hard about how to do that safely than have them improvise it under pressure.

r001.rationale: The response says not deploying is effectively not an option and that companies will deploy models despite uncertainty about scheming.

r002.rationale: It mentions enormous commercial and competitive pressures, but does not state that less cautious competitors will continue deploying.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention scheming AIs escaping into the outside world or the danger of stopping deployment after that.

astra-6.text:
Well, ideally we’d be able to establish that our models aren’t scheming before we use them for anything important. But we might not know how to do that. And I don’t think we should assume that, if we can’t establish that, everyone will simply refrain from deploying them. There could be enormous economic and strategic pressure to use these systems.

There’s also a more positive reason: these models might be extremely useful for making subsequent AI systems safer. We might want their help doing alignment research, evaluating other models, or building security measures. So refusing to use them could mean giving up tools that would substantially reduce the risk we face.

The question I’m interested in is: can we get useful work out of a model while ensuring that, even if it is trying to undermine us, it has very little opportunity to succeed? You might restrict what it can access, monitor its actions, and have its work checked by systems you trust more. None of that requires you to become convinced that its intentions are good.

That doesn’t mean you can safely use any model for any purpose. But having that option seems much better than being stuck choosing between trusting a potentially scheming model and forgoing its help entirely.

r001.rationale: It says we should not assume everyone will refrain from deployment if safety cannot be established, citing economic and strategic pressure.

r002.rationale: It mentions economic and strategic pressure to deploy, but does not identify less cautious competitors continuing deployment as the reason.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss scheming AIs escaping into the outside world or the danger of stopping deployment after that.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, ideally we’d be able to make models that we were confident weren’t scheming, and then use those. But I don’t think we can count on being in that position. We might have models that are extremely useful, including for doing AI safety research, without having good enough methods to establish that they’re actually trying to help us.

And in that situation, just saying “Well, don’t use them” has some pretty substantial costs. You might be giving up a lot of your ability to understand the next generation of AI systems or develop safeguards against them. And other people might go ahead and use these systems anyway, with fewer precautions.

So I want us to have a fallback: ways of getting useful work out of a model where our safety case doesn’t depend on trusting its intentions. You can try to restrict what it has access to, check its work, and arrange things so that attempts to cause harm are likely to get caught before they succeed. That’s the basic motivation for AI control. It’s not a claim that we can safely use arbitrarily powerful scheming models. It’s a claim that we should investigate how much safety we can get from those precautions, because we might really need them.

r001.rationale: The response says refusing to use the models has substantial costs and that others may use them anyway, so a serious scheming risk does not by itself mean deployment will stop.

r002.rationale: It identifies others using the systems with fewer precautions as a reason not to rely on simply refusing to use them.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss scheming AIs escaping into the outside world or the danger of stopping deployment after such an escape.
